title: GS 385 taro (NSIC G 9): Yield, Maturity and Characteristics
metaTitle: GS 385 taro: Yield, Maturity and Characteristics
metaDescription: GS 385 taro is a taro variety from PhilRootcrops, LSU (now VSU). See its days to harvest, yield, pest ratings, traits and where it grows best.
excerpt: GS 385 is a registered taro variety, also sold or known as NSIC G 9 or NSIC Gb 09. It was registered with the National Seed Industry Council (NSIC) in 2004 as NSIC 2004 Gb 09. It comes from PhilRootcrops, LSU (now VSU). It takes about 8 months from planting to harvest, with 8.85 tonnes per hectare on average in the trials.

blocks.text: If you came here looking for NSIC G 9 or NSIC Gb 09, this is the same taro. The facts below come from the NSIC registry kept by the Bureau of Plant Industry, with notes from its seller and farm sources. Compare it with the others in our [taro variety finder](/crop-varieties/taro), or see [every crop variety](/crop-varieties) we list. For the crop itself, read our guide: [Land preparation for root crops](/land-preparation/root-crop-land-preparation).

blocks.text: How long does it take, and how much does it yield?

GS 385 taro takes about 8 months from planting to harvest. That is about the average of the 10 taro varieties with a day count, 8 months. Count the months from planting, and plan the harvest for a dry stretch when you can.

Its average yield of 8.85 t/ha matches the average of its group, 8.82. Trial yields come from well managed plots, so your own will depend on water, fertilizer, pests and timing.

Once you know the day count, anee.io dates every task from each lot's own planting day, with [the growth stages and weather](/features/growth-stages-and-weather) beside it.
Is it resistant to pests and diseases?

blocks.caption: Reactions in the registry trials, rated under natural field conditions

blocks.text: It showed no weak spot in the ratings on record. Still, a resistant variety can break down when a new strain or pest population comes, so keep scouting.
The pests and diseases that hit taro fields most often: [cutworm](/pests/cutworm). Our [pest finder](/pests) and [disease finder](/diseases) help you name what you see.

Its roots have white with dominant streaks of purple fibers flesh and dark purple skin. Dry matter is 44.07 percent. A higher dry matter cooks mealy and gives processors more flour or starch from each tonne. It is recommended for food.
What its seller and farm sources say

items: **Fruit:** Dark purple skin, white flesh with strong purple fibre streaks, dry matter about 44 percent.
Registry lists it blight resistant, but PhilRootcrops later rated it worse for Phytophthora leaf blight than newer lines.

blocks.text: Why farmers know it: a dark purple gabi from PhilRootcrops with high dry matter. Check these against what farmers near you have seen, because the same variety can do differently from one town to the next.
Where and when to plant GS 385 taro
The registry recommends it for anywhere in the country. Gabi grows in wet lowland or on upland beds. Pick a variety for the land you have, and for the corm, the leaves or both.

items.q: Is NSIC G 9 the same as GS 385?
items.a: Yes. NSIC G 9 is another name for GS 385, registered as NSIC 2004 Gb 09. Seed sellers use both, so ask for either one.

items.q: How long does it take to harvest?
items.a: It takes about 8 months from planting to harvest. Then the weather and your care decide the exact day.
The record shows 8.85 tonnes per hectare on average in the trials. Your own yield depends on the soil, water, fertilizer and pests on your farm.
The registry recommends it for anywhere in the country. Ask your municipal agriculturist how it has done in your town.

items.q: Where can I buy seed of GS 385?
items.a: Ask an accredited seed dealer in your province, the seller named on this page or your municipal agriculturist. Look for the certified seed tag or a sealed pack before you pay.
